interest:
I study JWST observations of high-redshift galaxies and AGN, especially
little red dots (LRDs), compact red sources, dust-reddened or broad-line AGN,
early black-hole growth, and galaxy/AGN co-evolution at cosmic dawn.

Prioritize papers about:
1. JWST/NIRCam/NIRSpec/MIRI observations of high-redshift galaxies and AGN
2. little red dots, compact red galaxies, obscured AGN, broad-line AGN, and
   high-redshift black hole candidates
3. SED fitting, spectroscopy, emission lines, photometric redshifts, stellar
   masses, dust attenuation, AGN contamination, and source classification
4. high-redshift galaxy formation, reionization-era galaxies, early SMBH
   growth, and galaxy/AGN co-evolution
5. survey papers from CEERS, JADES, UNCOVER, COSMOS-Web, PRIMER, GLASS,
   RUBIES, and similar JWST deep fields

Also keep papers about AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs),
large multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, anomaly detection,
automated classification, spectral/photometric inference, or research agents
when they are applied to astronomy, astrophysics, JWST data, galaxy surveys,
AGN selection, or literature/data analysis.

Deprioritize unrelated stellar, solar-system, local-universe, gravitational
wave, or purely theoretical papers unless they directly inform high-redshift
galaxies, AGN, JWST analysis, or AI-for-astronomy workflows.

papers.title: Chaotic accretion can (still) explain early supermassive black hole growth
papers.subjects: Astrophysics of Galaxies (astro-ph.GA) ; Cosmology and Nongalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)
papers.abstract: The origin of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) is still debated, with hypotheses ranging from massive seeds to super-Eddington growth to chaotic accretion. Recent discoveries of very high redshift SMBHs constrain their possible origin and growth scenarios. We investigate whether the chaotic accretion scenario can explain the most extreme high-redshift SMBH masses. We predicted the exponential growth timescale of black holes accreting chaotically in a slowly-spinning dark matter halo, in which uncorrelated gas inflows maintain a low spin and hence a low radiative efficiency. We compared this prediction against the growth timescales and seed masses implied by a compilation of all known SMBH mass estimates at $z>7$ and against the feeding and feedback conditions expected in such haloes. We found that in the period $7.6 < z < 10.6$, the most massive SMBHs likely grew very efficiently, with an exponential growth timescale $\tau \sim 32$~Myr, which is consistent with chaotic accretion predictions provided that growth was almost continuous. All high-redshift SMBHs with virial mass estimates could have grown from seeds with $M_{\rm seed} \lesssim 100 \, \msun$. We describe the evolution of the mass reservoir feeding such a black hole, suggesting that wind-driven feedback eventually removes most of the gas and changes the growth mode of black holes at $z \sim 7.5$. We make several predictions regarding the spins, host-galaxy correlations, and observable counterparts of high-redshift SMBHs that distinguish our model from its alternatives. These predictions will be testable in the near future. Chaotic accretion from stellar-mass seeds remains a viable origin for the earliest known SMBHs, without invoking massive seeds or super-Eddington growth.
papers.Reasons for match: This directly addresses early supermassive black hole growth at z>7, a core part of my research on early black-hole growth and galaxy/AGN co-evolution at cosmic dawn.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks whether chaotic accretion can explain the most extreme high-redshift SMBH masses given recent z>7 discoveries. It finds that in 7.6<z<10.6 the most massive SMBHs could grow with an exponential timescale of ~32 Myr from seeds below 100 solar masses, consistent with chaotic accretion if growth was nearly continuous. This is highly relevant to my work on early SMBH growth and provides testable predictions for high-redshift AGN observations, though it is theoretical rather than JWST-based.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the compilation of z>7 SMBH mass estimates and their uncertainties
Check the assumptions about radiative efficiency, spin, and gas supply in the chaotic accretion model
Assess the predicted observables (spins, host-galaxy correlations) and whether they are testable with JWST
Look for how the model distinguishes itself from massive-seed and super-Eddington scenarios

papers.title: Halo Mass Function Constraints on Early Galaxy and AGN Populations in the JWST Era
papers.subjects: Cosmology and Nongalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO) ; Astrophysics of Galaxies (astro-ph.GA)
papers.abstract: The discovery by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) of massive galaxies and luminous active galactic nuclei (AGN) at high redshift provides an increasingly sensitive test of the connection between cosmological structure formation and the astrophysical processes that make dark matter halos observable. We develop a framework connecting the linear matter power spectrum to the mass variance, peak height, halo mass function (HMF), cumulative halo abundance, and observable galaxy and AGN populations. We use the Sheth-Tormen (ST) HMF as the baseline and compare it with an illustrative Bolshoi-Klypin-calibrated modification (KST) to quantify the sensitivity of predictions to the calibration of the HMF against cosmological N-body simulations. We apply the framework to three complementary tests: the baryonic and stellar mass reservoir available to massive galaxies, the abundance of halos capable of hosting luminous AGN, and the rest frame ultraviolet luminosity function of high redshift galaxies. Because the most massive systems occupy the rare, high peak tail of the halo distribution, modest changes in inferred host mass, baryonic conversion efficiency, black-hole occupation or duty cycle, and HMF calibration can produce large changes in predicted abundances. The ST-KST comparison shows that uncertainty in the high redshift halo population can materially affect the inferred host supply, particularly toward large z (10). Comparison with representative JWST massive galaxy, AGN, and UV luminosity function measurements demonstrates that matching the properties of an individual source is not sufficient for population consistency; the corresponding host halos must also exist in adequate numbers. Current observations provide increasingly stringent quantitative stress tests of both cosmological halo abundances and the baryonic and black hole physics at cosmic dawn.
papers.Reasons for match: It directly addresses JWST-era massive galaxies and luminous AGN at high redshift through halo mass function constraints, relevant to early galaxy/AGN populations and cosmic-dawn structure formation.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks whether halo mass function predictions can consistently accommodate JWST massive galaxies and luminous AGN at high redshift. It develops a framework linking the linear power spectrum to halo abundance and shows that modest changes in host mass, baryonic efficiency, BH occupation, or HMF calibration strongly affect predicted abundances. This matters for interpreting JWST AGN and massive-galaxy candidates, including whether their host halos exist in sufficient numbers at cosmic dawn.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for quantitative comparisons to JWST AGN and massive-galaxy abundance measurements
Check assumptions about BH occupation fraction, duty cycle, and baryonic conversion efficiency
Examine how ST versus KST halo mass function choices change high-z predictions
Look for implications for individual luminous AGN or LRD candidates at z>8

papers.title: Hierarchical Black Hole Mergers at High Redshift: Predictions for LISA and LGWA from SEEDZ
papers.authors: Daxal H. Mehta , Lewis R. Prole , John A. Regan , Rüdiger Pakmor , Sophie Koudmani , Ricarda S. Beckmann , Michael Tremmel , John H. Wise , Martin A. Bourne , Ralf S. Klessen , Simon C. O. Glover , Martin G. Haehnelt , John Brennan , Pelle Van De Bor , Debora Sijacki , Paul C. Clark
papers.subjects: Astrophysics of Galaxies (astro-ph.GA) ; Cosmology and Nongalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)
papers.abstract: We investigate the hierarchical assembly of black holes (BHs) in the early Universe using the next-generation SEEDZ cosmological zoom-in simulations. Our suite follows two independent regions (\textsc{Rarepeak} and \textsc{Normal1}) evolved with three BH feedback prescriptions: no feedback (NoFB), weak feedback (WeakFB), and standard thermal isotropic feedback (FidBH). Focusing on BH mergers at $z \geq 10$, we explore merger-driven BH growth and detectability with next-generation gravitational-wave observatories. We find that stronger AGN feedback models dramatically suppress hierarchical BH assembly compared to weaker feedback implementations. In the NoFB simulations, BHs frequently undergo repeated mergers, with some experiencing more than 50 merger events within a few hundred Myr and gaining over $10^8,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$ through mergers alone. In contrast, BHs in the FidBH simulations rarely undergo more than three mergers. NoFB therefore represents an upper limit to BH merger-driven growth beyond what is expected in the Universe. The suppression of BH mergers in the FidBH case is not driven by differences in galaxy assembly, BH occupation fractions, or BH seed abundances, which remain broadly similar across the simulation suites. Instead, feedback disrupts the dense gas surrounding newly formed BH seeds, suppressing their early accretion-driven growth and preventing them from entering runaway hierarchical merger pathways. Our results demonstrate that early-Universe feedback prescriptions strongly influence hierarchical BH growth through both mergers and accretion, producing distinct high-redshift merger populations. Coupled with seeding choices and other BH subgrid prescriptions, this introduces multiple degeneracies that will need to be broken in advance of LISA and other next-generation GW facilities.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper uses cosmological simulations of early black-hole seeding and merger-driven growth at z>=10, directly relevant to early SMBH growth and galaxy/AGN co-evolution, though it is simulation-focused rather than JWST observational.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks how AGN feedback prescriptions affect hierarchical black-hole assembly and merger rates at high redshift. It finds that strong feedback suppresses repeated mergers, while no-feedback models produce runaway merger-driven growth, creating distinct high-redshift merger populations. For my work, this informs theoretical expectations for early black-hole growth and the seeding/feedback degeneracies that JWST AGN and LRD observations may help constrain.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the predicted BH mass function and merger rates at z>=10 for comparison with JWST black-hole candidates
Look for how feedback prescriptions affect BH occupation fractions and accretion-driven growth
Check whether the simulations make any predictions relevant to LRD or compact AGN demographics

papers.title: Radiation pressure powers quasar broad absorption line winds but fails to drive galaxy feedback
papers.authors: Braden Seefeldt-Gail , Lluís Mas-Ribas , Norman Murray
papers.abstract: Most cosmological simulations invoke quasar-driven winds as the primary mechanism quenching star formation in massive galaxies, assuming wind momentum flux approaches the radiation-pressure maximum, $L/c$. Using 81,388 broad absorption line troughs from the SDSS-IV DR16 quasar catalog and detailed mock trough spectra, we detect line locking, a spectral signature of radiation-pressure-driven outflows, in 60 to 70 percent of troughs, demonstrating that radiative line driving dominates wind acceleration and ruling out alternative mechanisms. Direct measurement of the wind energy budget yields a median kinetic luminosity of only 0.01 percent of bolometric luminosity, 50 times below the level required for effective feedback. Line-driven quasar winds are therefore insufficiently powerful to quench star formation, challenging the primary physical mechanism invoked for black hole feedback in galaxy formation models.
papers.Reasons for match: This is a quasar broad-absorption-line wind and AGN feedback study using SDSS data; it directly addresses AGN physics and galaxy/AGN co-evolution, though not at high redshift or with JWST.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks whether radiation-pressure-driven quasar winds can provide the feedback needed to quench star formation in massive galaxies. Using 81,388 BAL troughs from SDSS-IV DR16, it detects line locking in 60-70% of troughs but finds the median kinetic luminosity is only 0.01% of bolometric luminosity, far below feedback requirements. This challenges a primary mechanism invoked in galaxy-formation models and is relevant to my interest in AGN feedback and galaxy/AGN co-evolution, though it is not a high-redshift or JWST study.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the line-locking detection statistics and how they constrain radiation-pressure driving
Check the kinetic-luminosity estimates and assumptions about outflow geometry and distances
Assess whether the feedback conclusions are extrapolated to high-redshift quasar populations
Look for any discussion of obscured or broad-line AGN relevant to LRD interpretations

papers.title: The $\mathrm{[O\ III]}\lambda5007$ Equivalent Width as an Ionization-Parameter Diagnostic Across Cosmic Time
papers.authors: Dian P. Triani , Lisa J. Kewley
papers.abstract: Nebular emission lines and stellar continua probe the conditions of $\mathrm{H\ II}$ regions. The optical emission line $\mathrm{[O\ III]}\lambda 5007$ is important because it is observable across a wide redshift range, enabling studies of interstellar medium (ISM) conditions across cosmic time. We investigate the equivalent width of $\mathrm{[O\ III]}\lambda 5007$ (EWO3) as an ionization-parameter diagnostic, providing an alternative to the $\mathrm{[O\ III]} \lambda 5007 / \mathrm{[O\ II]} \lambda 3727$ (O32) ratio, which requires broad wavelength coverage and dust corrections that may not be available at high redshift. We employ the MAPPINGS photoionization code with input spectra from \textsc{BPASS}, comparing single-star and binary-inclusive stellar populations. We find that binary-inclusive populations sustain harder ionizing spectra and strong $\mathrm{[O\ III]}\lambda 5007$ emission to later ages than single-star populations. EWO3 is highly sensitive to the ionization parameter and exhibits systematic dependencies on metallicity, gas pressure, and stellar population age. While these dependencies broadly follow those of O32, EWO3 is less sensitive to gas pressure in the low-metallicity, high-ionization regime, making EWO3 well suited for studies of metal-poor and high-redshift galaxies. Comparing the models with observations, we find that local galaxies are reproduced by lower-pressure models, whereas intermediate- and high-redshift galaxies require higher gas pressures, indicating evolving ISM conditions across cosmic time. We present metallicity- and pressure-dependent calibrations of EWO3 as an ionization-parameter diagnostic. When validated against ionization parameters derived from O32, the $\log(P/k)=6$ calibration provides the best agreement for local galaxies, while the $\log(P/k)=7$ calibration best reproduces intermediate- and high-redshift galaxies.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper develops the [O III]λ5007 equivalent width as an ionization-parameter diagnostic for high-redshift galaxies, directly relevant to JWST emission-line studies and ISM conditions. It connects to my interest in SED fitting, emission lines, and high-redshift galaxy classification.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks whether [O III]λ5007 equivalent width can serve as an ionization-parameter diagnostic alternative to O32 across cosmic time. The main claim is that EWO3 is highly sensitive to ionization parameter and less pressure-dependent than O32 in the low-metallicity high-ionization regime, with calibrations favoring higher gas pressures at high redshift. It matters for my work because JWST high-redshift galaxies often lack the broad wavelength coverage needed for O32, so EWO3 could be a practical diagnostic for ISM conditions and AGN contamination in LRDs and compact sources.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the EWO3 calibrations as functions of metallicity and gas pressure, and whether they are applicable to JWST wavelength coverage.
Check whether the paper provides diagnostics that separate AGN from star-forming ionization in high-redshift sources.
Look for comparisons with observed high-redshift galaxy samples and whether the pressure evolution is supported by JWST data.
Assess whether the BPASS binary-inclusive models change the inferred ionization parameters for metal-poor galaxies.

papers.title: Galaxy merger-driven signatures in massive black hole pair hosts across cosmic time
papers.authors: Pranav Satheesh , Aklant K. Bhowmick , Laura Blecha
papers.abstract: Galaxy mergers can drive gas toward galactic nuclei, enhancing both star formation and black hole accretion in post-merger galaxies. Here we use the IllustrisTNG-50 simulation and two boxes from the BRAHMA simulation suite, all of which adopt different black hole formation models, to characterize merger-associated signatures in candidate massive black hole (MBH)-pair hosts. In all three simulations, we select post-merger galaxies whose progenitors both host MBHs and quantify their enhancements in star formation and black hole accretion relative to matched non-merging controls. In TNG50, we find substantial merger-triggered enhancements in both specific star formation rate (sSFR) and specific black hole accretion rate (sBHAR) at $0 \leq z < 3.3$, reaching $\sim 1.4\times$ and $\sim 1.5-1.7\times$ the controls, respectively. The BRAHMA runs employ more physically motivated seed formation models, seeding BHs in lower-mass galaxies and at higher redshifts than TNG50. In BRAHMA, merger-driven enhancements in sSFR and gas fractions are comparable to those in TNG50 at $z \lesssim 3.3$ and persist to the highest redshifts probed by BRAHMA ($z \sim 6$). Despite this, BRAHMA shows no significant merger-driven enhancement in sBHAR across its entire redshift range. In a similar vein, TNG50 pair hosts show an enhanced AGN fraction relative to matched controls, whereas BRAHMA shows only a weak excess among the most rapidly accreting MBHs.
papers.Reasons for match: It addresses merger-driven black-hole accretion and MBH-pair hosts across cosmic time, connecting galaxy/AGN co-evolution and high-redshift BH growth, though it is simulation-based rather than JWST observational.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks how galaxy mergers enhance star formation and black-hole accretion in massive black-hole pair hosts. Using IllustrisTNG-50 and BRAHMA, it finds merger-driven sSFR enhancements persist to z~6 but sBHAR enhancements depend strongly on BH seeding and are absent in BRAHMA. This informs expectations for JWST-detected dual or accreting black holes at cosmic dawn and the role of seeding models in interpreting high-z AGN.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for predicted AGN fractions and sBHAR enhancements at z>4 relevant to JWST AGN samples
Check how BH seeding prescriptions affect observable dual-AGN or pair-host signatures
Examine whether the simulations make testable predictions for JWST compact red sources or LRDs

papers.title: The Role of the Cosmic Web in Galaxy Evolution Across 0.4<z<4
papers.authors: Sina Taamoli , Bahram Mobasher , Hossein Hatamnia , Nima Chartab , John R. Weaver , Ghassem Gozaliasl , Anton M. Koekemoer , Caitlin M. Casey , Jeyhan S. Kartaltepe , Aryana Haghjoo , Olivier Ilbert , Henry J. McCracken , David B. Sanders , Nicholas Scoville , Sune Toft
papers.abstract: We investigate the dependence of stellar mass and star formation activity on the topology of hosting large-scale structures using mass-complete galaxy samples in four redshift bins spanning from z = 0.4 to z = 4 using the COSMOS2020 catalog. Cosmic web components (clusters, filaments, and field) are identified by applying the Multiscale Morphology Filter to galaxy density maps, and group memberships (central, satellite, isolated) are assigned to each galaxy by the Friends of Friends (FoF) algorithm. Out to z < 1, we find that stellar mass increases toward denser structures, driven primarily by central and satellite galaxies, with differences up to ~0.35 dex between field and clusters. At these redshifts, star formation rate (SFR) is suppressed by ~0.1 dex in clusters compared to field galaxies, particularly for centrals, while the SFR of star-forming galaxies shows a much weaker dependence on the type of host structure, indicating that the quenched population primarily drives the observed environmental dependence. Specific SFR (sSFR) shows the strongest decline for centrals in clusters at z<1, consistent with enhanced quenching in dense environments. At 1<z<2, star formation activity becomes largely independent of environment, suggesting a transitional regime in the role of large-scale structure. At z>2, we observe a mild increase in SFR (~+0.1 dex) and sSFR (~+0.13 dex) from field to cluster galaxies, pointing to a possible reversal of environmental trends during early cosmic epochs. These results highlight the evolving influence of environment on galaxy evolution and set the stage for deeper investigations with upcoming wide-field surveys.
papers.Reasons for match: This is a COSMOS2020 study of environment-dependent galaxy evolution out to z=4, relevant to high-redshift galaxy formation and survey science but not specifically JWST, LRDs, or AGN.
papers.Short digest: The paper investigates how stellar mass and star formation activity depend on cosmic-web topology from z=0.4 to z=4 using COSMOS2020. It finds environmental quenching at z<1, a transitional regime at 1<z<2, and a mild reversal toward enhanced star formation in clusters at z>2. This is relevant to my interest in high-redshift galaxy formation and survey-based environmental studies, though it lacks JWST data and AGN/LRD focus.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the mass-completeness limits and how they affect the z>2 environmental trends
Look for whether AGN contamination is addressed in the SFR or mass estimates
Assess whether the cosmic-web classification could be applied to JWST deep fields like COSMOS-Web
Check the significance of the claimed reversal of environmental trends at z>2

rules: Prioritize JWST studies of high-redshift compact broad-line emitters, including compact blue broad-line emitters (BLEs), even when the title does not mention AGN or little red dots.

Include papers connecting blue broad-line sources to LRDs through ionizing continua, emission lines, obscuring envelopes, escape fractions, or contributions to reionization. Relevance does not require red colors or a confirmed AGN interpretation.

examples.title: The ionizing properties of JWST's compact broad-line emitters
examples.authors: Sara Mascia , Jorryt Matthee , Alberto Torralba , Jenny E. Greene , Anna-Christina Eilers , Edoardo Iani , Rohan P. Naidu
examples.abstract: The recent JWST discovery of a numerous population of broad-line emitters (BLEs) at $z>4$ has reopened the question of whether sources other than faint galaxies contributed significantly to cosmic reionization. To assess this contribution, we present a systematic census of compact, blue broad-line emitters at $4\leq z\leq7$ selected from the DJA, designed to isolate sources in which the UV continuum and the broad-line emission originate from the same compact physical region. Starting from a parent sample of 4145 galaxies with NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy and NIRCam imaging, we apply criteria on broad Ha emission (FWHM$>2000$km s-1, detected at S/N$\geq5$, complete at $L_{Ha,broad}\geq10^{42.7}$erg s-1), blue continuum slopes ($\beta_{UV}\leq-1.5$, $\beta_{opt}<0.5$), and morphological compactness in both the rest-frame UV and optical, returning a final sample of 20 sources. This constitutes $\sim20%$ of the PRISM-selected broad-line sample, which is dominated by Little Red Dots (LRDs). We find that the compact blue BLEs display hot ionizing continua, high-ionization UV lines (CIV, NIV], HeII), and elevated Lya emitter fractions ($X_{Lya}=50-67%$) relative to star-forming galaxies and LRDs. Beyond their similar lack of X-ray emission, their optical spectra closely resemble those of LRDs. This suggests that compact blue BLEs extend this population towards lower column density envelopes, but with similar engines, rather than representing a physically distinct population. Using Sirocco to model physical configurations that reproduce the observed spectra, we find a high ionizing photon production efficiency (log$\xi_{ion}\sim25.4$Hz erg-1) and a weighted average escape fraction $fesc\sim0.2$ for the bluest sources, and $\sim0.01$ for LRDs. This implies that broad-line sources do not dominate reionization globally, but given their luminosity, their contribution can dominate up to few Mpc scales.
